ut.title: Ultrasonic Thickness Testing & UT Inspection | Boston, MA
ut.description: Ultrasonic testing in Boston, MA: waterfront tank and hull thickness, boiler and vessel readings, shear-wave weld UT. Technicians travel to site. Get a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Gauging in Boston, Massachusetts
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Boston-area facilities for ultrasonic thickness gauging and shear-wave weld examination. Typical scopes include waterfront fuel tanks and piping, vessels and boilers in hospitals and laboratories, marine steel at repair berths, crane and structural welds, and fabrication shop work. Send the asset list and the governing code through the quote form and we reply within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Boston

Greater Boston is a harbor, a research hub and an old industrial city at once, and ultrasonic testing follows all three. On the water, the container terminal in South Boston, the bulk and petroleum terminals along the Mystic River and Everett waterfront, and the fuel depots on the Chelsea River all depend on steel that sits in salt air and cycles through wet and dry conditions. A large dry dock at the former Navy annex in South Boston has repaired ships for the Military Sealift Command, which puts hull plate and tank boundaries within the same commercial harbor.

Inland, the demand is different. Hospitals, university campuses and the region's large life-science sector run steam boilers, chilled-water systems, compressed-air receivers and stainless process piping. Utility and district energy plants add high-pressure steam and feedwater lines. The older building stock and river crossings bring structural steel whose welds were made decades ago. Ultrasonic testing measures remaining wall and examines weld volume across all of that, and our general ultrasonic testing page explains the technique before this page narrows to Boston.

What UT will and will not tell you about Boston steel

A thickness reading answers one question: how much metal remains under the probe. It does not say what caused the loss. On a waterfront tank shell, thinning near the bottom course often comes from water collecting at the foot and from corrosion under the coating, while a uniform loss across the roof plate points to atmospheric attack. On a marine tank boundary, pitting under failed coating can leave a surface that looks sound and a back wall that does not. Readings taken in a grid reveal those patterns, and a grid is more valuable than a single point.

Boston's older buildings add another twist. Steam and hot-water systems installed decades ago may have been repaired in sections, so a single run can contain pipe of different wall thicknesses, different grades and different weld practices. A technician who simply reads a thickness and compares it with a nominal schedule can misjudge a segment that was never schedule pipe in the first place. We ask for any drawings, past reports and repair history and, when none exist, we measure and record the as-found wall so that the next survey has a real baseline instead of an assumption.

Weld examination reads reflections from a shear-wave beam. Planar flaws such as cracks and lack of fusion give strong echoes, while rounded porosity gives weak ones, so the technician evaluates amplitude, length and position together. UT has limits: it needs a prepared surface and a couplant, it struggles with coarse-grained cast material and some thick stainless welds, and it cannot find a tight crack lying parallel to the sound beam. When the real concern is surface cracking, magnetic particle inspection in Boston or liquid penetrant testing in Boston is the better tool, and we will say so rather than sell UT for the wrong job.

Massachusetts rules and the codes behind the readings

Pressure equipment in Massachusetts falls under the Board of Boiler Rules, a five-member board within the Department of Fire Services that issues regulations under 522 CMR. The same code family covers air tanks and unfired pressure vessels, and 522 CMR 15.00 adopts the National Board Inspection Code, which governs repairs and alterations. State inspectors and insurance company inspectors decide whether equipment may operate. Atlantis supplies the thickness data and weld findings that support their decision, and does not take their place.

For the examination itself, the references are ASME Section V, Article 4 for welds and Article 5 for materials, with SE-797 in Article 23 covering contact thickness measurement. Acceptance comes from the construction or repair code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 and its Appendix 12 for vessel welds, ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel. For tanks and piping already in service, API 653 and API 570 apply when the owner has adopted them, and the owner's authorized inspector holds responsibility for those programs. Our guide to ultrasonic testing covers the physics in more depth.

Running a thickness survey on a Boston asset

The plan comes first: the owner and the technician agree which locations are measured, how many readings make up each, and how they are numbered so next cycle's data lines up with this one. On pitted or rough steel we use a dual-element probe, because separate transmitting and receiving crystals handle uneven back walls better than a single crystal. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of matching material, and checked again during and at the end of the job, so drift is caught instead of buried.

Coatings and scale are the usual obstacle. Thick coatings on marine and tank steel can be read through only after the procedure is qualified for them, and many jobs require local removal at each point. Salt crust and rust scale are removed to bright metal, and the surface is smoothed so the probe seats flat. On curved pipe, the probe's contact face must match the diameter or readings scatter. Readings are logged directly against the location ID, and any value below the owner's retirement thickness is reported immediately so the owner can act without waiting for the final document.

Shear-wave examination of welds

Angle-beam examination follows a written procedure. The technician calibrates on a reference block, builds a distance-amplitude curve using side-drilled holes, and scans the weld from both sides where access allows, sweeping the beam across the fusion zone and root. Probes of 45, 60 and 70 degrees are chosen by plate thickness and joint geometry. Scanning sensitivity is raised above the reference level to catch small reflectors, and each indication that exceeds the recording threshold is sized and located relative to a reference point on the weld.

Boston projects often have tight access. Pipe racks over water, vessels in crowded mechanical penthouses and structural members on active sites limit probe positions, and in those cases the technician records which scan positions could not be reached so the owner knows the actual coverage. A weld map with weld numbers, scan sides and notes about limitations travels with the report. Where the code calls for it, an acceptance statement against the specific table is added for every recorded indication.

For repaired welds the sequence matters. We examine the original weld, then the excavation if a defect was ground out, then the finished repair, and we make sure each stage is referenced to the same weld number so the history stays readable. Owners who track weld repair rates for a fabricator or a welding crew find that ultrasonic examination of production welds gives an early indication of drift, which is cheaper to correct on the third joint than on the thirtieth.

Who performs the work and who signs the report

Technicians who set up the equipment, scan and interpret are Level II under Atlantis NDT's written practice, built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level III approves the procedures and reviews finished reports. That reviewer is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Because SNT-TC-1A places certification with the employer, each report names the technician and level, so you can show your own inspector or insurer who did the work.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 for its quality and environmental management systems. If your own team needs help with written practices or procedure writing before an audit, our Level III consulting can step in.

What the report contains

  • Asset and location identification keyed to your drawing, isometric or tank course sketch.
  • Procedure number, revision and code edition, with the acceptance criteria used.
  • Instrument, probe, calibration block, couplant and the calibration checks made during the job.
  • Thickness tables or grids with nominal, minimum and measured values, and low readings highlighted.
  • Weld indications with position, length, amplitude, depth, a sketch and an accept or reject conclusion.
  • Technician and Level III names and levels, plus a statement of any areas not examined and why.

The aim is a file that can be understood years later by someone who was not on site, including a state inspector reviewing history for a unit that has changed hands.

Planning a UT job in Boston

New England weather dictates much of the planning. In winter, water-based couplant freezes on outdoor steel, so glycerin or gel couplant is used, cables stiffen, batteries drain faster and a probe carried from a warm vehicle to frozen pipe drifts until it settles. Wind off the harbor is a practical problem on tank roofs and pipe racks. In summer, humidity and salt air speed surface rust, and dark steel in sun gets hot enough to need a high-temperature probe and couplant. Nor'easters and storm surge can close waterfront sites, so alternate dates are discussed up front. On vessels at a repair berth, tank cleaning and gas-free certification come first, since technicians cannot enter or work in a tank until the owner's marine chemist or competent person has cleared it, and thickness work is scheduled to follow that step rather than compete with it.

Waterfront terminals require security credentials and safety orientation, and some berths and fuel facilities restrict equipment and ignition sources. Hospitals and laboratories restrict work hours and require infection-control and clean-area procedures. Atlantis has no office in Boston, so technicians travel to your site with calibrated equipment; we build lodging and shipment into the schedule and propose a sequence that keeps readings comparable across multiple buildings or tank groups.

UT, MT or PT for your Boston scope

Choose UT for wall loss and for weld volume. Choose MT for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, and PT for stainless steel, aluminum and other nonmagnetic metals, such as the stainless process systems common in life-science plants. A repair on a waterfront vessel might use UT to map wall around a defect, MT to confirm the crack is gone after grinding, and UT again on the completed weld. Our MT versus PT comparison helps with the surface-method choice.

Training your own UT technicians

Boston employers with in-house inspectors can build capability through UT Level 1 training, UT Level 2 training and the ultrasonic simulator for hands-on practice. Local options are on our NDT training in Boston page.

faq.q: Does Atlantis NDT have an office in Boston for ultrasonic work?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Boston. Level II technicians travel to your facility with calibrated equipment and a written procedure, and we plan travel, lodging and shipment into the schedule when we quote the job.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness on a waterfront fuel tank?
faq.a: Yes, at agreed locations on shell courses, roof plates and nozzles, after the surface is cleaned. The data supports the owner's inspection program; the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for tank decisions and intervals.

faq.q: Who regulates boilers and pressure vessels in Massachusetts?
faq.a: The Board of Boiler Rules, within the Department of Fire Services, makes the rules under 522 CMR, and state or insurance inspectors decide whether equipment may operate. Atlantis supplies the examination data those inspectors use.

faq.q: How does cold weather affect UT readings in Boston?
faq.a: Water couplant freezes on cold steel, so glycerin or gel is used. Probes moved from a warm vehicle drift until they settle, and batteries drain faster. We calibrate at working temperature and re-check during the job.

faq.q: Can you gauge through coatings on marine steel?
faq.a: Sometimes. A thin, well-bonded coating can be read through when the procedure has been qualified on a sample, and the coating thickness is recorded. Thick or blistered coating is removed at each test point.

faq.q: What standard do you use for ultrasonic weld examination?
faq.a: We write the procedure to ASME Section V, Article 4 and apply the acceptance table of the governing code, such as ASME B31.3, Section VIII Division 1, or AWS D1.1. Before work begins, the owner or engineer tells us which code governs.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a weld in Boston?
faq.a: Only where the code, the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector all agree beforehand. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, but we can examine welds ultrasonically where the code accepts it.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my staff in ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Yes, with Level 1 and Level 2 theory courses and a simulator. Your employer certifies technicians under SNT-TC-1A, so experience hours, vision checks and practical examinations are completed and signed by the employer.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Testing & MPI Inspection | Boston, MA
mt.description: Mag particle testing in Boston, MA: waterfront cranes, harbor steel, vessel and boiler repairs, shop welds. Technicians travel to your site. Request a quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) in Boston, Massachusetts
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Boston-area sites for magnetic particle testing of ferromagnetic steel: cranes and lifting gear on the waterfront, marine and harbor structures, pressure vessel and boiler repairs, and weld work in fabrication shops. MT shows surface and slightly subsurface cracks directly on the part. Send the component, code and access details through the quote form; we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing is used in Boston

The Boston waterfront is a heavy-lifting environment. The container terminal in South Boston runs ship-to-shore cranes and rubber-tired gantry cranes, and the bulk terminals up the Mystic River run their own heavy handling equipment. All of that is welded steel under repeated load and exposed to salt air, so fatigue cracks at pedestals, boom joints, spreader attachments and lug welds are the failures inspection exists to catch. At the ship repair end of the harbor, the work is steel renewal and crack repair on hull structure, rudder and shaft supports, and deck fittings.

Away from the water, MT is used on pressure equipment and building steel. Hospitals, universities and laboratories maintain boilers, vessels and air receivers, and after a weld repair the excavation and the finished weld are examined by MT. Older river crossings and rail structures carry riveted and welded steel from different decades, where repairs must be proven crack-free before they go back into service. Our magnetic particle testing page covers the method in general; the sections below cover what it takes in Boston.

What MT detects and what it misses

The method depends on magnetism. A steel part is magnetized, and if a crack breaks the surface the field leaks out of the part at the crack. Fine iron particles gather at the leak and mark it as a sharp line. Because the effect depends on the part being strongly magnetic, MT is used on carbon and low-alloy steel and cast steel, but not on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum or copper alloys. Stainless parts, which are common in laboratories and pharmaceutical plants around Boston, call for liquid penetrant testing instead.

MT sees only the near surface. A crack buried deep in a thick weld does not leak enough field to show, and ultrasonic testing is the better tool for that. Orientation matters too: a crack running along the field direction can be invisible, which is why the method requires examination in two directions. Heavy coatings, rust and weld spatter reduce sensitivity. A good technician prepares the surface, picks the technique to match the discontinuity the owner worries about, and reports what the examination can and cannot rule out.

Massachusetts rules that surround MT repairs

When MT supports a repair on a boiler or pressure vessel, the state framework decides who accepts the work. The Board of Boiler Rules, part of the Department of Fire Services, issues regulations under 522 CMR, and 522 CMR 15.00 adopts the National Board Inspection Code, which governs repairs and alterations to pressure-retaining items. The state inspector or the insurer's inspector accepts or rejects the repair; the NDT contractor does not. We therefore write MT reports so that the procedure, technique and acceptance criteria can be checked by that inspector without a phone call.

The technique references are ASME Section V, Article 7 and ASTM E1444 for the practice, with ASTM E709 as the guide. Acceptance depends on the construction code: ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping, ASME B31.1 for power piping, and AWS D1.1 for structural steel and many crane structures. Where the owner follows API 510 or API 570, the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the program, and we supply the NDE results. The Article 7 explainer goes through the technique requirements line by line.

Edition control is a recurring point in Massachusetts. A repair package can name one edition of Section V, the vessel's original construction code another, and the NBIC edition adopted by the Commonwealth a third. We ask for all three at scoping, write the MT procedure to the combination that the jurisdiction and the owner accept, and cite the editions on the first page of the report, so no one has to guess which printing of a rule was applied to a particular weld.

Techniques we use in the field and the shop

The choice starts with the magnetizing equipment. For most field jobs, an articulated electromagnetic yoke is the tool: it magnetizes by placing two legs on the surface, needs no direct current through the part and leaves no arc burns. Under Article 7 an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and we verify lifting power before work and record it. For castings and forgings in a shop, a bench unit with a coil or head-and-tail contacts gives circular and longitudinal fields in one setup.

Particles can be dry powder, which is easy to use and holds up on rough weld surfaces outdoors, or wet particles in a liquid bath, which give better sensitivity on smooth parts. Fluorescent wet particles show hairline cracks under UV-A light but need a dark area, and a harbor-side crane deck in daylight does not give one without a tent. A residual field is checked and, where it could interfere with welding, machining or sensitive equipment nearby, the part is demagnetized and the result recorded. A field indicator shows that the magnetic field reaches the area of interest and runs in the intended direction.

Cold, damp and salty: conditions on Boston MT jobs

Boston weather changes how MT is done. In winter, wet baths thicken as oil carriers cool and water baths can freeze, so concentration is checked by settling test at working temperature, and dry powder replaces wet particles on some outdoor jobs. Ice, frost or condensation on steel must be removed because particles cannot form an indication over a wet film. Salt air and spray leave residue that clogs particles and creates background, so surfaces are wiped and, where needed, rinsed and dried.

Surface temperature has limits too. Freshly welded steel must cool to the procedure limit, or a qualified technique for elevated temperature is used. Hot summer decks on a waterfront crane can exceed what dry powder tolerates. Darkness is the other constraint: in December, daylight ends early, which suits fluorescent work after hours when the site permits it. We build these conditions into the plan so the examination is done under the conditions the procedure assumes.

On crane structure specifically, a useful MT plan starts from a list of known fatigue locations: boom and portal joints, sill beam connections, corners of cutouts, the toes of attachment welds, trolley rail supports and lug welds on lifting points. Prior repair welds deserve special attention because they are where cracking tends to return. We examine these in a fixed order, record each against a numbered sketch, and flag any location that was blocked by guarding or by cable runs, so that a second entry can be planned with the owner's maintenance team instead of being forgotten.

Qualification and review

MT is performed by Level II technicians qualified under Atlantis NDT's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level III approves technique sheets and reviews reports, and the reviewer here is Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. SNT-TC-1A places certification with each employer, and our reports name the technician and level so your inspector can see who did the examination. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification, which governs how procedures and records are controlled.

Shops and plants that write their own MT procedures sometimes want a second pair of eyes. Our written practice development and Level III consulting services review MT procedures against the editions you are bound to.

What the MT record includes

  • Part or weld identification matched to your drawing, with crane or equipment serial where relevant.
  • Procedure number and revision, the standard and the acceptance code applied.
  • Magnetizing equipment, lifting-power check, particle type and carrier, and light level measured at the surface.
  • Surface condition, temperature, coating left on and preparation done.
  • Technician and Level III names and levels.
  • Indications by location, length and orientation, with a photograph or sketch, and an accept or reject conclusion.

For crane work, we also note which welds were not accessible, so the owner can plan an additional entry rather than assume full coverage. A grind-out repair is documented in three steps: the crack as found, the excavation after grinding, and the finished weld, each with its own MT result and a reference to the same weld number, so the repair history can be followed from one page of the file.

Planning an MT job in Boston

Several local practicalities matter. Waterfront terminals ask for security credentials and safety orientation and may limit ignition sources and hot work. Crane inspections are scheduled around vessel calls, so jobs often depend on a quiet window of a few hours at a berth. Hospitals and campuses control hours and noise. Nor'easters and storm surge can close a harbor site at short notice, so a backup date is useful. Access equipment, such as lifts, scaffolding or crane platforms, is usually provided by the owner or the general contractor.

Atlantis has no office in Boston, so technicians travel to your site with yokes, particles, lights and consumables. We agree beforehand on power, lighting, surface preparation and who provides access. For multi-asset programs, such as a set of cranes or a group of vessels, we propose an order that keeps procedure and reporting consistent.

Choosing between MT, PT and UT in Boston

MT suits carbon and low-alloy steel where surface cracks are the concern. Liquid penetrant testing in Boston suits stainless steel, aluminum and bronze, for example in laboratory process systems or aluminum marine structure. Ultrasonic testing in Boston suits wall loss and internal weld flaws. Many jobs use two or three together, and the complete MT guide helps decide which comes first.

Training your own MT technicians

Employers who want their own crew performing magnetic particle examinations can start with MT Level 1 training and move on to MT Level 2 training. Boston-area options appear on our NDT training in Boston page, and candidates can check their knowledge with the NDT practice tests.

faq.q: Can Atlantis NDT inspect waterfront cranes in Boston with MT?
faq.a: Yes, on the welds, pedestals and structural joints that are ferromagnetic and accessible. We agree the weld list and access with the owner, schedule around vessel operations, and report any welds we could not reach.

faq.q: Is MT suitable for stainless steel in Boston laboratories?
faq.a: Not for austenitic stainless steel, which is not magnetic. For stainless process piping and vessels we use liquid penetrant testing, which finds surface-breaking cracks in any non-porous material.

faq.q: Who accepts a pressure vessel repair in Massachusetts?
faq.a: The state inspector or the insurer's inspector accepts repairs under the Board of Boiler Rules framework and the National Board Inspection Code. We perform the MT and supply the record they rely on.

faq.q: Does cold weather stop magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: It changes the technique. Wet baths thicken or freeze, so we check concentration at working temperature, switch to dry powder where suitable, and make sure frost and condensation are removed before magnetizing the part.

faq.q: What yoke strength is required for MT?
faq.a: Under ASME Section V Article 7, an AC yoke must lift at least 10 pounds and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds at the maximum pole spacing used. We check this before each job and record the result.

faq.q: Can you use fluorescent particles at a harbor site?
faq.a: Yes, when we can darken the area with a tent or work after daylight. Fluorescent particles are examined under UV-A light, and the light level at the surface is measured and recorded.

faq.q: Do you demagnetize parts after MT?
faq.a: When the residual field could interfere with welding, machining, instruments or later operations, yes. The procedure states when demagnetizing is required, and we record the residual field reading when the check is made.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train our people in magnetic particle testing?
faq.a: Yes. We teach Level 1 and Level 2 MT theory and exam preparation. Your employer certifies its technicians under its own written practice, which holds the experience hours, vision checks and practical examinations.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Boston, MA | Liquid PT
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing in Boston, MA for stainless process piping, aluminum marine parts, castings and repairs. Technicians travel to site. Get a quote.
pt.h1: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Boston, Massachusetts
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II technicians to Boston-area plants, laboratories, shipyards and shops for dye penetrant inspection, formally liquid penetrant testing. PT finds cracks and other flaws that are open to the surface on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, bronze and machined parts that MT cannot examine. To scope a job, send the material, location and code via the quote form. We reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is used in Boston

Boston and Cambridge host one of the densest concentrations of life-science and laboratory facilities in the country, and those buildings run on stainless steel. Clean steam, purified water, process piping, bioreactor vessels and sanitary tanks are all stainless, and a crack in a weld or a repair is a contamination risk as well as a structural one. Hospitals add stainless steam and medical gas systems. Penetrant testing is the practical surface method for all of it, because stainless is not magnetic.

On the harbor side, aluminum workboats, ferries and the superstructure of larger vessels need weld and repair checks that do not rely on magnetism. Propellers, shafts and rudder fittings are bronze or stainless, and PT checks them during drydock and repair. Pump and valve bodies, castings and machined components in power and manufacturing plants add more. Our penetrant testing overview explains the technique at a national level; this page covers how it applies around Boston.

What PT shows and where it fails

Penetrant testing works by capillary action. A thin liquid with high wetting ability is applied to a clean surface and creeps into any opening. After a set time the surface liquid is removed, a developer is applied, and the developer draws liquid out of cracks and pits so that they appear as bright or colored marks. The method suits cracks, laps, seams, porosity open to the surface and lack of fusion that breaks out, on nearly any non-porous material.

Its limits come from the same mechanism. A flaw that is closed at the surface, whether because it lies below it or because metal has been smeared across it by grinding, machining or abrasive blasting, will not draw liquid in. Porous or very rough surfaces hold penetrant and produce false indications. Residual oil, coatings or paint block the opening. For wall loss or internal weld flaws, ultrasonic testing in Boston is the proper method, and on carbon steel magnetic particle testing in Boston is often faster and finds slightly subsurface cracks.

Codes and the Massachusetts framework

The procedure follows ASME Section V, Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the practice and ASTM E1417 covering the examination standard for fluorescent and visible systems. Acceptance is set by the governing construction or repair code: ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping, and the applicable AWS code where PT is permitted on structural or marine welds. Article 6 requires penetrant materials used on nickel-base alloys to be analyzed for sulfur and those used on austenitic stainless steel and titanium to be analyzed for halogens.

Pressure equipment adds the state layer. The Board of Boiler Rules, within the Department of Fire Services, makes rules under 522 CMR, and 522 CMR 15.00 adopts the National Board Inspection Code for repairs and alterations. The state or insurer's inspector accepts the repair. Atlantis evaluates indications against the code and reports them, and does not accept work on the inspector's behalf. Read more in our guide to the Article 6 requirements.

Choosing the penetrant system

Penetrants differ by type and method. Type II visible dye needs only white light and is the usual choice for field welds and repair excavations, with a solvent-removable process because it needs no water or power. Type I fluorescent penetrant is examined under UV-A light in a darkened area and reveals finer cracks, so it is used when the code or the component demands higher sensitivity. Water-washable and post-emulsifiable methods suit shop work on larger numbers of parts with an organized wash station.

Material compatibility drives many Boston decisions. Stainless piping in a pharmaceutical suite or a hospital needs low-halogen materials, and nickel alloys need low-sulfur ones, with lot certificates on file. Owners often also want penetrant residues removed and the cleaning recorded, because the surface goes back to product contact. For aluminum and marine alloys, the choice must also take account of coatings that will be applied afterward, since residual penetrant can spoil adhesion. The procedure states all of this before the first part is touched.

Castings and machined components bring their own considerations. Sand castings and rough surfaces hold penetrant in the texture and produce a heavy background, so the surface may be lightly machined or the wash step adjusted, and the acceptance standard is chosen to suit the casting grade. Machined pump and valve parts with tight tolerances cannot be abraded, so cleaning is chemical and the examination happens before any final coating. In each case the technician documents what was done to the surface, since an examination on a surface that was altered after a defect appeared tells you less than one on the as-received part.

Cleaning, dwell and development in practice

Good PT is mostly good cleaning. Weld spatter, scale, oil and paint come off the examination zone, using solvents and lint-free cloths, with mechanical methods limited to those that will not smear metal over a crack. The surface is then dried completely, because solvent or water left in a crack blocks penetrant. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left for the dwell time that the procedure requires for the material and flaw type.

Excess penetrant is removed with controlled technique, first with dry cloths and then lightly with dampened ones, never by flooding with solvent. The developer is applied as a thin, even coat, and interpretation takes place within the developer's time window. The technician evaluates bleed-out patterns, distinguishing round pores from linear cracks, and measures them against the acceptance criterion. Photographs with a scale are taken before the developer dries and the pattern fades. After the examination the part is cleaned to remove developer and penetrant.

The materials themselves are checked as well. A system performance check on a cracked reference panel shows whether the penetrant, remover and developer in use still reveal fine cracks, and old or contaminated materials are discarded. The panel check and the lot numbers go into the file together, so a reviewer can see that the examination was done with materials that were known to work on the day.

Temperature, humidity and damp conditions in Boston

Under ASME Section V, Article 6 the standard technique applies when the surface of the part and the penetrant are between 40 and 125 degrees Fahrenheit, roughly 5 to 52 degrees Celsius. Boston winters push outdoor pipe, tank and hull steel below that range for weeks. Cold penetrant thickens, enters fine cracks slowly, and a longer dwell cannot rescue a surface that is too cold. The remedy is either a heated enclosure that brings the part into range for the full dwell, or a non-standard temperature technique qualified on a comparator block.

Summer brings the opposite problem on exposed dark surfaces and in humid, salt-laden air. Penetrant can dry on a hot surface, and humidity condenses on cooled parts. Technicians measure surface temperature and record it with the times. Rain, spray and fog stop work outdoors, so waterfront PT is often organized around weather windows, and sheltered areas such as a drydock floor or a covered pier are preferred when possible.

Qualification and review

Level II technicians performing PT are qualified under Atlantis NDT's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, and a Level III reviews procedures and reports. Reports are reviewed by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Each employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so the report shows the technician's name and level and the date of the examination. Atlantis operates under ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates for document and environmental control.

If a laboratory or plant wants its penetrant procedure checked against a new code edition, our Level III consulting and written practice development teams can review it.

What a Boston PT report records

  • Component, weld or casting identification tied to your drawing or equipment tag.
  • Procedure, revision, governing standard and acceptance code, with the penetrant type and method.
  • Materials: brand, product and lot numbers of cleaner, penetrant and developer, with sulfur and halogen certifications where the base metal calls for them.
  • Surface preparation, part and material temperatures, dwell time, development time.
  • Technician and Level III names and levels.
  • Indications with location, size and type, photographs with a scale, and an accept or reject statement.

For pharmaceutical and clean-service systems, cleaning verification and residue removal are noted as well, so the owner's validation file stays complete.

Planning a PT job in Boston

Penetrant materials are solvent based and flammable, so work in laboratories, hospitals and mechanical rooms follows the owner's hot-work, ventilation and chemical approval rules. Clean-area and infection-control procedures in healthcare and life-science buildings may restrict materials, work hours and waste handling, and the owner should state them at scoping. Shipyards and terminals have credential and safety orientation requirements. Plan for the fact that PT is slower than MT, as dwell and cleaning take time, and stage multi-weld jobs so that cleaning, application and examination overlap.

Atlantis has no office in Boston, so technicians travel to your site with lot-controlled consumables and a UV-A lamp when fluorescent work is called for. A short call before mobilizing settles materials, power, lighting, temperature expectations and the cleaning standard, so the crew arrives with the right system.

PT, MT or UT for your Boston work

Use PT for stainless, aluminum, nickel and bronze, and where a part cannot be magnetized. Use MT on carbon and low-alloy steel when you want speed and slightly subsurface sensitivity. Use UT for remaining wall and internal weld quality. The MT versus PT comparison gives a quick decision table, and many Boston scopes pair PT on the weld surface with UT on the wall.

Training your own PT technicians

Penetrant testing is a practical first method for new technicians. Atlantis teaches it in PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, and students can practice interpretation in the penetrant testing simulator. Boston-area details are on our NDT training in Boston page.

faq.q: Can dye penetrant inspection be used on aluminum boat welds in Boston?
faq.a: Yes. PT works on aluminum, which is not magnetic. We clean the weld, apply penetrant, develop and examine, and record indications. Coatings planned afterward are considered, because residues can affect adhesion.

faq.q: Do penetrant materials need to be low in halogens for stainless steel?
faq.a: Yes. ASME Section V Article 6 requires materials used on austenitic stainless steel and titanium to be analyzed for halogens, and those used on nickel alloys for sulfur. We use documented lots and record them.

faq.q: How cold is too cold for liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard technique applies from 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and materials. Below 40 we heat the part with an enclosure, or use a technique qualified at the lower temperature on a comparator block.

faq.q: Does PT find cracks below the surface?
faq.a: No. PT detects only discontinuities open to the surface. For internal flaws or wall loss we use ultrasonic testing, and we often combine the two on a vessel, pipe or marine weld.

faq.q: Is fluorescent penetrant better than visible dye?
faq.a: Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and reveals finer cracks, but needs a darkened area and UV-A lamp. Visible dye is simpler in the field. The procedure sets which system applies to your component.

faq.q: Can you leave the part clean for product contact?
faq.a: Yes. After examination we remove developer and penetrant residues with approved cleaners and record the cleaning, which matters in pharmaceutical, food and clean-service systems where the surface returns to product contact.

faq.q: Who accepts a repair after PT in Massachusetts?
faq.a: The state or insurer's inspector accepts repairs on boilers and pressure vessels under 522 CMR and the National Board Inspection Code. Atlantis performs the PT and reports indications against the code for that inspector.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my staff in liquid penetrant testing?
faq.a: Yes. We teach Level 1 and Level 2 penetrant theory and offer a simulator for practice. Your employer certifies technicians under its written practice, so experience hours, vision checks and practical examinations remain with the employer.

rt.title: Radiographic Testing in Boston, MA: Alternatives to RT
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Boston, MA we can discuss UT as a volumetric option, Level III review of images and RT theory courses.
rt.html:
Anyone searching for radiographic testing in Boston deserves a direct answer first: Atlantis NDT does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity governed by Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules, 10 CFR Part 34, or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State. Massachusetts is one of those states. Because we hold no radiography service here, we say so rather than leave the question open.

Three related things are available to Boston owners and contractors, and they cover most of what an RT search is really after: ultrasonic examination as a volumetric option where the code allows it, independent Level III review of radiographs produced by a licensed contractor, and classroom theory for radiography.

Ultrasonic examination where the code accepts it

Radiography and ultrasonic testing both examine the inside of a weld. UT uses shear-wave probes and a calibrated reference, has no exclusion zone, and does not interrupt neighboring trades. On a crowded Boston site, such as a hospital plant room, a laboratory fit-out or a harbor-side pipe rack, that can simplify scheduling considerably.

Whether UT may replace RT is a code decision and a contract decision. Process piping under ASME B31.3 and pipeline welds under API 1104 each have ultrasonic provisions, structural groove welds under AWS D1.1 have their own UT acceptance rules, and ASME Section VIII permits UT in lieu of RT only when particular conditions are satisfied. The substitution must be agreed with the owner, the engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job. Details of our service are on ultrasonic testing in Boston, and you can describe your welds through the quote form.

Reviewing radiographs and radiography procedures

Pressure piping, vessels and structural work in Massachusetts frequently arrive with radiographs from a licensed contractor, and the owner or general contractor then wants an independent opinion. Our Level III goes through film or digital images, the technique sheet and exposure records, checking them against ASME Section V, Article 2 and the construction code. Because the reviewer works with images and paperwork, no source is handled and no radiation licence is involved.

Review can also mean a second read on a disputed indication or an audit of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice before work starts. That work is done by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, who can read the images without ever handling a source. Explore the format on our NDT Level III consulting page, or use written practice development if your company needs its own documents.

Training and surface methods

Companies that want to build radiography knowledge in-house can use our radiographic testing Level 2 course for theory. Radiation safety licensing is a separate matter handled by the state and the licensed employer, and the course does not replace it. For Massachusetts employers, our NDT training in Boston page lists the options.

For surface cracking in steel, magnetic particle testing in Boston covers ferromagnetic metals, and liquid penetrant testing in Boston covers stainless steel, aluminum and nickel alloys. Atlantis has no office in Boston, so technicians are mobilized to your site for these methods. See our inspection services in Massachusetts page for the full list of conventional services.

What to send to scope a Boston alternative

To scope a UT alternative or an image review quickly, gather the weld list with material grade and thickness, the drawing or isometric, the code and edition named in the contract, the acceptance criteria and any wording that mandates radiography. If radiographs already exist, a few sample images and the technique sheet tell the reviewer how big the review is. Tell us also about site constraints, such as occupied areas or restricted hours, which often decide which method is practical.

faq.q: Can Atlantis NDT do radiography in Boston?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under NRC or Agreement State rules and is not a service we offer. We provide ultrasonic testing, image review and theory training.

faq.q: Can UT stand in for radiography on Massachusetts pressure piping?
faq.a: Only when the construction code, the owner, the engineer and the authorized inspector agree before the work. Some codes include ultrasonic provisions for production welds, others do not, so the code position is checked first.

faq.q: Can your Level III review radiographs from another company?
faq.a: Yes. The Level III can read film or digital images alongside the technique sheets, measuring them against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, offer a second opinion on contested indications, and review the contractor's procedure.

faq.q: Does reviewing radiographs require a radiation licence?
faq.a: No. Review involves images and records, not a radiation source. The licensed contractor who exposed the film or captured the images stays responsible for the radiography itself and for radiation safety.

faq.q: Can I take a radiography theory course from Atlantis?
faq.a: Yes. We teach radiographic testing theory in a Level 2 course. It does not cover radiation safety licensing, which stays with the state and the licensed employer, and your employer certifies technicians under its written practice.
